title: Rust Foundations
description: Read, run and write small Rust programs with the real compiler checking your work, from printing and variables to ownership, enums, traits and iterators.
audience: Someone new to Rust. Some programming in another language helps but isn't needed. Systems Programming picks up from here, so this course stays on the language itself and leaves memory layout, threads and unsafe code to that course.
outcomes: You'll be able to read a short Rust program and predict exactly what it prints.
You'll be able to write functions, loops and decisions that compile and produce the output you meant.
You'll be able to explain why a value was moved or a borrow was refused, name the error code (E0382, E0502, E0499, E0597), and fix it.
You'll be able to model data with structs and enums, and handle missing values and failures with Option, Result and ?.
You'll be able to store data in Vec, String and HashMap, and write generic functions, traits and closures.
You'll be able to combine these pieces into a program of about fifty lines that parses data, skips bad input and prints a report.

lessons.title: Printing and naming values
lessons.objective: Read a short Rust program, predict what it prints, and use println!, let, mut and shadowing correctly.

concepts.title: Bindings
concepts.summary: let attaches a name to a value; the name cannot be reassigned unless it is declared mut, and a second let with the same name creates a new binding that shadows the first.

misconceptions: Thinking let x = 5; x = 6; is allowed. Bindings are immutable by default, and rustc reports E0384.
Treating shadowing as mutation. let x = x * 2 makes a new binding, which is why it may even change the type.
Forgetting the ! in println!. It is a macro, and println("hi") is a different, missing function.
sequence: A program is fn main() { ... } and println! writes a line of text.
Placeholders: {} and {name} take values from the arguments or from variables in scope.
let gives a value a name. Types are inferred.
Run a program that assigns twice and read E0384, then add mut.
Shadowing: a new let reuses the name, can change the type, and ends with its block.
Predict, then run: the habit for the rest of the course.
examples: let x = 5; let x = x * 2; println!("{x}"); prints 10.
let spaces = "   "; let spaces = spaces.len(); makes spaces the number 3.
let mut count = 1; count += 1; count += 1; leaves count at 3.

figures.learnerAction: Predict the two lines, then run.
Add the one word that fixes it, and run again.

lessons.title: Numbers, types and functions
lessons.objective: Choose a number type, predict integer arithmetic, read a function signature and write a small function.

concepts.title: Functions and types
concepts.summary: Every function parameter and return value has a stated type, the types of operands must match exactly, and the last expression of a body without a semicolon is the return value.

misconceptions: Expecting 7 / 2 to be 3.5. Dividing two integers truncates toward zero and gives 3.
Believing Rust converts i32 to i64 or to f64 for you. It never does; you write the conversion, and rustc reports E0308.
Adding a semicolon to the last line of a function. The semicolon turns the value into a statement, the body returns (), and rustc reports E0308.
sequence: Integer types (i32, u8, usize) and floats (f64), and why the default integer is i32.
Integer division and remainder: 7 / 2 is 3, 7 % 2 is 1, -7 / 2 is -3.
Mixing types fails: an i32 and an i64 do not add. Convert with as.
fn name(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32: reading a signature as a contract.
Expressions and statements: the last line without a semicolon is the value.
Write a function and call it from main.
examples: let a: i32 = 5; let b: i64 = a; fails with E0308; let b = a as i64; works.
fn double(n: i32) -> i32 { n * 2 } returns 2n; fn double(n: i32) -> i32 { n * 2; } fails.

figures.learnerAction: Change the type of wide to i32 and read what rustc says.
Delete the semicolon and run again.

lessons.title: Making decisions with if
lessons.objective: Write if / else if / else, use the value of an if as an expression, and explain why its condition must be a bool and its branches the same type.

concepts.title: if is an expression
concepts.summary: An if / else evaluates to the value of the branch that runs, so it can sit on the right of let or be the last line of a function, provided every branch has the same type.

concepts.title: Conditions are bool
concepts.summary: The condition of an if must have type bool; Rust never treats numbers or strings as true or false.

misconceptions: Writing if count { ... } the way C or Python would. A number is not a bool, and rustc reports E0308.
Putting a semicolon after the value in a branch. The branch then yields () and no longer matches the other one.
Leaving out else while using the if as a value. With no else the missing branch would be (), so rustc reports E0317.
sequence: if condition { ... } else { ... } with a bool condition built from ==, <, >=, && and ||.
Else-if chains test in order and stop at the first branch that is true.
Because if is an expression, let kind = if n % 2 == 0 { "even" } else { "odd" };.
Both branches must produce the same type: read the E0308 for 1 versus "one".
A function whose body is just an if chain, with no return keyword.
Predict, then run: guard clauses and boundaries such as >= versus >.
examples: n = 7: let kind = if n % 2 == 0 { "even" } else { "odd" }; prints 7 is odd.
fn grade(score: u32) -> char with 90 giving 'A', 80 giving 'B', otherwise 'C': grade(85) is 'B'.
let x = if true { 1 } else { "one" }; fails with E0308.
let x = if true { 1 }; fails with E0317.

figures.shows: A box labelled 'condition: bool' with two arrows leaving it, 'true' to a block holding "even" and 'false' to a block holding "odd". Both blocks feed one slot labelled 'value of the if', which is bound to kind. A second view shows the same slot with an i32 block and a &str block and a red cross on the slot.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between the matching-types view and the mismatched-types view.

lessons.title: Repeating work with loops and ranges
lessons.objective: Choose between loop, while and for, write ranges with and without their end value, and use break to stop or to return a value.

concepts.title: loop, while and for
concepts.summary: loop repeats until break and may break with a value, while repeats as long as a bool condition holds, and for visits each item of an iterator such as a range.

concepts.title: Ranges
concepts.summary: a..b runs from a up to but not including b, a..=b includes b, and methods such as rev() and step_by(n) change the order and spacing.

misconceptions: Reading 1..5 as 1 to 5 inclusive. It stops at 4; 1..=5 includes 5.
Using a C-style for (i = 0; i < n; i++). Rust has no such form; for walks an iterator.
Using the loop variable after the loop. It exists only inside the body, and rustc reports E0425.
sequence: loop with a counter and break; break can carry a value: let r = loop { ... break n; };.
while condition { ... } for a loop that depends on a changing value.
for i in 1..4 visits 1, 2, 3; for i in 1..=4 visits 1, 2, 3, 4.
(1..=3).rev() counts down; (0..10).step_by(3) gives 0, 3, 6, 9.
Count the iterations of a range before running: end minus start, plus one if inclusive.
The loop variable is scoped to the body.
examples: let mut n = 0; let r = loop { n += 1; if n * n > 50 { break n; } }; r is 8.
for i in (1..10).step_by(3) prints 1, 4, 7.
Sum of 1..=5 is 15; sum of 1..5 is 10.
while n > 0 { n -= 1; } with n starting at 3 runs three times.

figures.shows: Two number lines from 0 to 6. The first marks 1..4 with a filled dot at 1 and an open dot at 4. The second marks 1..=4 with filled dots at 1 and 4. Dots between them are filled in both.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the right end of the range between 3 and 6 and watch the number of filled dots change.

lessons.title: Ownership and moves
lessons.objective: State the three ownership rules, predict which assignments and calls move a value, and fix a use-after-move with clone or by returning ownership.

concepts.title: Ownership
concepts.summary: Every value has exactly one owner; when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped, and assigning or passing a non-Copy value to a function moves ownership.

concepts.title: Copy and move
concepts.summary: Simple fixed-size types such as integers, bool and char are copied on assignment; a String or Vec is moved, so the old name cannot be used afterwards.

misconceptions: Assuming let b = a; copies the String like it would in Python or Java. It moves, and a can no longer be used (E0382).
Thinking a function call just 'looks at' its argument. Passing a String by value gives the function ownership.
Cloning everywhere to silence the compiler. clone copies the text, which costs time; references (next lesson) usually are the better answer.
sequence: Why a language needs a rule for who cleans up: a String owns text it must free.
The three rules: each value has an owner, one owner at a time, dropped when the owner leaves scope.
let s2 = s1; moves; reading s1 afterwards is E0382 'borrow of moved value'.
Integers, bool and char are Copy: let b = a; leaves both usable.
Passing to a function moves; returning a value hands ownership back.
clone() makes a second independent value when you really need one.
examples: let a = 5; let b = a; a + b is 10 because i32 is Copy.
let s1 = String::from("hello"); let s2 = s1; println!("{s1}") fails with E0382.
fn shout(mut s: String) -> String { s.push('!'); s } called as let w = shout(w); keeps a usable w.
let v = vec![1, 2, 3]; let w = v; v.len() fails with E0382.

figures.shows: Two views of the Rust code let s1 = String::from("hello"); let s2 = s1;. Before: a small box s1 pointing to a text strip h-e-l-l-o. After: the s1 box greyed out with a cross, a new box s2 pointing to the same strip. A caption names the strip 'the String's text' and does not discuss the stack or heap.
figures.learnerAction: Step between before and after.
Change one line to w = v.clone() and run again.
Predict the output first.

lessons.title: References and borrowing
lessons.objective: Pass values by & and &mut, and explain with the borrow rules why rustc reports E0502, E0499 or E0596.

concepts.title: References
concepts.summary: &x borrows x without taking ownership, &mut x borrows it for changing, and * follows a reference to the value.

concepts.title: The borrow rules
concepts.summary: At any moment a value may have any number of shared references or exactly one mutable reference, never both, and a reference may not outlive the value.

misconceptions: Thinking & means copy. A reference is a view of the same value, so reading through it sees later changes only if the borrow rules allow them.
Believing a borrow lasts to the end of the block. It lasts until the reference's last use, so reordering two lines can make an E0502 disappear.
Forgetting mut at both ends: the variable must be let mut and the borrow must be &mut x, otherwise E0596.
sequence: A function that takes String moves it; fn len(s: &String) -> usize borrows it and the caller keeps the value.
&mut: fn add(v: &mut Vec<i32>) and the call add(&mut v); * to change a plain number through a reference.
Rule one: many shared references may exist together.
Rule two: one &mut excludes every other reference; read E0499 for two &mut and E0502 for & plus &mut.
A borrow ends at its last use, so a shared reference printed before a push is fine.
Trying to change through a shared reference is E0596.
examples: let mut x = 5; bump(&mut x); bump(&mut x); with fn bump(n: &mut i32) { *n += 1; } leaves 7.
let first = &v[0]; v.push(4); println!("{first}") fails with E0502.
let r1 = &mut s; let r2 = &mut s; used together fails with E0499.
let r = &s; println!("{r}"); let m = &mut s; compiles, because r is no longer used.

figures.shows: A horizontal timeline of the lines of a short program. A bar for the variable v runs the whole length. A green bar labelled &v starts at the line 'let first = &v[0]' and ends at the line that prints first. A red marker at the line 'v.push(4)' falls inside the green bar. A second view moves the print above the push, so the green bar ends before the red marker.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the print line above or below the push and see whether the bars overlap.
Delete one of the pushes and see whether it still fails.
Predict both lines.

lessons.title: Slices, String and &str
lessons.objective: Take slices of arrays and strings with ranges, tell String from &str, and explain why a string cannot be indexed by position.

concepts.title: Slices
concepts.summary: A slice such as &[i32] or &str is a borrowed view of part of a sequence, written &x[a..b], and it keeps the whole sequence borrowed while it is in use.

concepts.title: String and &str
concepts.summary: String owns growable UTF-8 text, &str borrows text that someone else owns (a literal or a String), and len() counts bytes, not characters.

misconceptions: Expecting s[0] to give the first letter. Text is UTF-8, so one character can take several bytes; rustc reports E0277 and you use chars() or a byte range instead.
Believing len() counts letters. "héllo".len() is 6 because é takes two bytes.
Taking &String as a parameter. &str accepts both a String and a literal, so it is the better parameter type.
sequence: An array slice &a[1..4] has length 3 and shares the array's elements.
A string slice &s[0..5] is a &str; a literal "hi" is already a &str.
String versus &str: owner versus view; String::from, &s, .as_str().
fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str as a function that accepts both.
Why s[0] is rejected, and what to use: s.chars().nth(0), s.bytes(), s.chars().count().
A slice holds the borrow: clearing the String while a word slice is alive is E0502.
examples: "héllo".len() is 6 and "héllo".chars().count() is 5.
first_word("hello world") is "hello"; first_word("single") is "single".
let c = s[0]; fails with E0277: the type str cannot be indexed by an integer.

figures.shows: The text hello world as eleven numbered cells 0 to 10. A bracket under cells 0 to 4 is labelled &s[0..5] with 'start 0, length 5'. A second bracket under cells 6 to 10 is labelled &s[6..11]. The String s is drawn above as the owner of all eleven cells.
figures.learnerAction: Change the two range ends with sliders and see which cells the bracket covers.
Change the word and predict both counts.

lessons.title: Structs and methods
lessons.objective: Define a struct, give it methods and an associated constructor in an impl block, and choose between self, &self and &mut self.

concepts.title: Structs
concepts.summary: A struct groups named fields into one type, and a value of it is built with Name { field: value }.

concepts.title: Methods
concepts.summary: Functions in an impl block whose first parameter is self, &self or &mut self are called with dot syntax, while functions without self, such as new, are called with Name::.

misconceptions: Assuming every method takes ownership. &self borrows, so area() can be called repeatedly; only self consumes.
Expecting a struct to be changeable field by field when its binding is not mut (E0594).
Expecting println!("{}", p) to work for a struct. A struct has no Display by default; derive Debug and print with {:?}.
sequence: struct Rect { w: u32, h: u32 } and building one: Rect { w: 30, h: 50 }.
Fields read with dot, and written only if the binding is mut.
impl Rect { fn area(&self) -> u32 { self.w * self.h } } and r.area().
&self reads, &mut self changes, self consumes.
Associated functions: Rect::square(4) built with Self.
#[derive(Debug)] and {:?} / {:#?} to look at a value; tuple structs for a single wrapped value.
examples: Rect { w: 30, h: 50 }.area() is 1500.
Rect { w: 8, h: 7 }.can_hold(&Rect { w: 5, h: 3 }) is true.
#[derive(Debug)] struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 } prints Point { x: 1, y: 2 }.
struct Celsius(f64) with to_fahrenheit: 100 gives 212.0.

lessons.title: Enums and match
lessons.objective: Define an enum whose variants may carry data, and use an exhaustive match, with guards and ranges, to compute a value from it.

concepts.title: Enums
concepts.summary: An enum is a type whose value is exactly one of its named variants, and each variant may carry its own data.

concepts.title: match
concepts.summary: match compares a value against patterns in order, binds the data inside a variant, must cover every case, and is an expression whose arms share one type.

misconceptions: Thinking an enum is a list of integer constants. Rust variants can hold different data, and they are not numbers unless you say so.
Adding a catch-all _ arm to quiet the compiler. It hides the case you will later add, so use it only when 'everything else' really is one case.
Believing match falls through like switch. Only the first matching arm runs.
sequence: enum Coin { Penny, Nickel, Dime, Quarter } and a value Coin::Dime.
match coin { Coin::Penny => 1, ... } as an expression returning cents.
Exhaustiveness: remove an arm and read E0004 'patterns not covered'.
Variants with data: Shape::Rect { w, h }, Shape::Circle(r), and binding the data in a pattern.
Guards and ranges: n if n < 0, 1..=9, and _ for the rest.
Methods on an enum with impl.
examples: Coin value_in_cents: 1, 5, 10, 25.
Shape::Rect { w: 3.0, h: 4.0 } has area 12.
describe(n): negative below 0, zero, small for 1..=9, large otherwise.
A traffic light cycling Red, Green, Yellow, Red.

lessons.title: Option: a value that may be missing
lessons.objective: Use Option<T> for values that may be absent, and unpack it with match, if let, unwrap_or and let-else instead of null checks.

concepts.title: Option
concepts.summary: Option<T> is the standard enum with two variants, Some(value) and None, used wherever a value may be absent, and it is a different type from T so the absence cannot be forgotten.

concepts.title: Unpacking an Option
concepts.summary: match and if let run code for Some(x) and optionally for None, unwrap_or gives a default, and unwrap stops the program if the value is None.

misconceptions: Using an Option as if it were the value inside (Some(3) + 1). rustc reports E0369, and that is the point: you must decide what happens for None.
Reaching for unwrap whenever rustc complains. unwrap on None ends the program, so prefer match, if let or unwrap_or.
Thinking None means 0 or empty. It means no value, and 0 is a perfectly good Some(0).
sequence: Why a language without null needs a type for 'maybe': Option<i32> is not an i32.
Functions that may fail to produce a value return Option: v.get(i), text.chars().next(), find.
match opt { Some(x) => ..., None => ... }.
if let Some(x) = opt { ... } when only one case matters, and let-else for early exit.
unwrap_or(default), and what unwrap does on None.
Write your own function that returns Option.
examples: vec![10, 20, 30].get(1) is Some(20); .get(5) is None.
"42".parse::<i32>().ok() is Some(42); "4x2".parse::<i32>().ok() is None.
first_even(&[1, 3, 4, 6]) is Some(4); first_even(&[1, 3]) is None.
safe_divide(10, 2) is Some(5); safe_divide(1, 0) is None.

lessons.title: Errors with Result and ?
lessons.objective: Return Result<T, E> from a function that can fail, propagate errors with ?, and decide between handling an error and letting the program panic.

concepts.title: Result
concepts.summary: Result<T, E> is an enum with Ok(value) for success and Err(error) for failure, so a function that can fail says so in its return type and the caller must deal with both.

concepts.title: The ? operator
concepts.summary: Placing ? after a Result gives the Ok value or returns the Err from the current function immediately, and it works only in a function whose return type can carry that error.

misconceptions: Thinking Rust has exceptions that fly up the stack by themselves. An error is an ordinary value; ? returns it explicitly, and you can see every place it can happen.
Using ? in main when main returns (). rustc reports E0277, because there is nowhere to send the Err.
Using unwrap to 'handle' errors. unwrap panics, which is right for 'this can only be a bug', and wrong for bad user input.
sequence: "42".parse::<i32>() returns Ok(42) and "abc" returns Err(ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit }).
match on a Result, and printing the error with {}.
Write fn parse_and_double(s: &str) -> Result<i32, ParseIntError>.
? as 'unwrap or return early', and how it shortens a sequence of fallible steps.
Where ? is allowed: functions returning Result or Option; fn main() -> Result<(), E>.
panic, unwrap and expect for bugs; Result for failures a caller can handle.
examples: "12".parse::<i32>() prints Ok(12) with {:?}.
parse_and_double("21") is Ok(42); parse_and_double("x") is Err(ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit }).

lessons.objective: Store and change data with Vec<T>, String and HashMap<K, V>, and use the entry API to count items.

concepts.title: Vec
concepts.summary: Vec<T> is a growable list of values of one type, built with vec![] or Vec::new(), extended with push, read with v[i] (which panics out of range) or v.get(i) (which returns an Option).

concepts.title: HashMap
concepts.summary: HashMap<K, V> stores values under keys, insert replaces, get returns an Option, entry(key).or_insert(default) inserts only when the key is absent, and the iteration order is not specified.

misconceptions: Writing for x in v and then using v. A for loop over v itself consumes it (E0382); iterate over &v to keep it.
Relying on the order of a HashMap when printing. It is unspecified and can differ between runs; sort the keys first.

lessons.title: Traits and generics
lessons.objective: Define a trait, implement it for your own types, and write a generic function or struct whose type parameter is limited by trait bounds.

concepts.title: Traits
concepts.summary: A trait names behaviour as a set of method signatures, with optional default bodies, and a type opts in with impl Trait for Type.

concepts.title: Generics and trait bounds
concepts.summary: A generic function or struct is written once for any type T, and a bound such as T: PartialOrd + Copy states which operations the body may use on T.

misconceptions: Expecting a generic function to accept any operation. Inside fn bigger<T>(a: T, b: T), nothing is known about T, so a > b fails with E0369 until you add T: PartialOrd.
Thinking a trait is a class with fields. A trait holds only behaviour; data stays in the struct.
Believing generics cost speed at run time. Rust generates a specialised copy for each concrete type, so there is no lookup.
sequence: Two types with the same method idea (area) and why a shared name is not enough.
trait Area { fn area(&self) -> f64; } and impl Area for Square.
A default method that calls another method of the trait.
A generic function fn largest<T>(v: &[T]) -> T, and the E0369 that tells you what the body needs.
Bounds: T: PartialOrd + Copy; the same bound written with impl Trait or a where clause.
A generic struct Pair<T> with an impl that has bounds.
examples: trait Speak with name() and a default greet() that returns I am followed by the name.

lessons.title: Lifetimes in signatures
lessons.objective: Explain why a function returning a reference needs a lifetime annotation, write 'a on functions and structs, and read E0106, E0597 and E0515.

concepts.title: Lifetimes
concepts.summary: A lifetime is the span of code in which a reference is valid, and the compiler checks that no reference is used after the value it points to is gone.

concepts.title: Lifetime annotations
concepts.summary: A signature such as fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str relates the output reference to the inputs so the caller's code can be checked; it does not extend how long anything lives.

misconceptions: Thinking 'a makes a value live longer. It only describes a relation that already exists; the compiler rejects code where the relation is false.
Believing every reference needs an annotation. Elision rules fill them in when there is one input reference, or &self.
Returning &s for a local String. The String is dropped at the end of the function, so the reference would dangle (E0515).
sequence: A dangling reference: a pointer to something already gone, which Rust refuses to compile.
Shorter scope: let r; { let x = 5; r = &x; } println!("{r}"); is E0597.
Two input references and one output: which does the result borrow from? fn longest without annotations is E0106.
fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str: the result lives no longer than the shorter input.
Why fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str needs no annotation: the elision rules.
Structs that hold references: struct Excerpt<'a> { part: &'a str }.
examples: longest("kiwi", "plum") with >= returns "kiwi" for equal lengths.
longest("rust", "go") is "rust".
A function that returns &s for a local s fails with E0515.
Excerpt { part: first sentence } cannot outlive the novel it borrows from.

lessons.title: Closures and iterators
lessons.objective: Write closures that capture variables and chain iterator methods such as map, filter, sum and collect to turn one collection into another.

concepts.title: Closures
concepts.summary: A closure |x| expression is a small unnamed function that can use variables from the place where it is written, and move captures them by ownership.

concepts.title: Iterator adaptors and consumers
concepts.summary: Adaptors such as map and filter describe a transformation lazily, and nothing runs until a consumer such as sum, count or collect asks for the items.

misconceptions: Expecting map to run immediately. Without a consumer nothing happens (and rustc warns that iterators are lazy).
Thinking a closure's parameter types can change between calls. The first call fixes them, and a second call with another type is E0308.
Using iter() when you meant into_iter(). iter() yields references, so filter closures see &i32 and need care.
sequence: A closure: let add = |a, b| a + b; and one that uses a local: let f = |x| x + offset.
Iterators: (1..=5), v.iter(), and for as the simplest consumer.
map and filter, then collect::<Vec<_>>() or sum::<i32>().
Laziness: print inside map and watch the order of output.
Chains read like a pipeline: filter(...).map(...).sum().
move closures and returning a closure with impl Fn.
examples: vec![1, 2, 3].iter().map(|x| x + 1).collect::<Vec<i32>>() is [2, 3, 4].
words.iter().map(|w| w.len()).collect() turns ["rust", "go", "c"] into [4, 2, 1].
fn make_adder(n: i32) -> impl Fn(i32) -> i32 { move |x| x + n }.

concepts.title: Composing a program
concepts.summary: A small program is a handful of types and functions where Result carries bad input to one place that decides what to do, collections hold the data, and the borrow rules shape who owns what.

concepts.title: Modules
concepts.summary: mod name { ... } groups items, and pub makes one visible outside its module, so code outside calls it as name::item.

misconceptions: Putting everything in main. Small functions with clear types (parse_line, mean) can be tested by reading them alone.
